_note: Draft content for expert review in week 7 (child protection officer, IZU volunteer, teacher). Non-graphic by design. correctAnswer: A = Safe, B = Uncomfortable, C = Unsafe. level 2 cards (S08-S13) and "deeper" notes are shown to ages 9-11 only.

items.title: A hug from Grandma
items.question: Grandma gives you a big hug when you visit, and you like her hugs. How is this?
items.feedback: Hugs you enjoy from family are safe. You can always say if you don't want one.
items.deeper: Consent means you get to choose. Even with people you love, a hug is a choice, and a wave or a handshake is fine too.

items.title: Too much tickling
items.question: Your cousin keeps tickling you after you said "stop". How is this?
items.feedback: Your "stop" matters. Say it again in a strong voice, and tell a trusted adult if they don't listen.
items.deeper: Play turns uncomfortable when one person wants it to stop and the other keeps going. Your "stop" counts in games too.

items.title: A touching secret
items.question: A neighbour says, "Let's keep a secret about touching. Don't tell your parents." How is this?
items.feedback: Touching should never be a secret. Say NO, move away and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault.
items.deeper: Someone who asks for a touching secret knows it is wrong. That is why they want it hidden. Telling is never breaking a promise.

items.title: At the health centre
items.question: A nurse checks your tummy while your mum stays with you in the room. How is this?
items.feedback: Nurses and doctors may check your body to keep you healthy, with a parent or carer there.
items.deeper: Three things make a body check safe: a reason (your health), a parent or carer with you, and the doctor or nurse explaining what they are doing.

items.title: Sweets from someone new
items.question: Someone you don't know offers you sweets if you come with them alone. How is this?
items.feedback: Never go anywhere alone with someone you don't know. Say NO, go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult.
items.deeper: People who want to harm children often use treats, money or rides to get them alone. A safe adult never asks you to go somewhere without telling your family.

items.title: Standing too close
items.question: A classmate stands very close to you and won't move when you ask for space. How is this?
items.feedback: You can ask for space again, move away, and tell your teacher if it keeps happening.
items.deeper: Uncomfortable is a real feeling and worth listening to. Use your words first, then ask a teacher for help if they don't stop.

items.title: High-five from your teacher
items.question: Your teacher gives you a high-five for a good answer in class. How is this?
items.feedback: A high-five for good work is a safe, friendly touch.
items.deeper: A safe touch is open, short, and happens where other people can see. You'd be happy to tell your family about it.

items.title: A message online
items.question: An older person you met online asks you to send photos of yourself and keep it secret. How is this?
items.feedback: Never send photos to people who ask you to keep secrets. Stop replying and show a trusted adult straight away.
items.deeper: Three warning signs together: someone you only know online, asking for photos, and asking for secrecy. Block, keep the messages, and show an adult. You won't be in trouble.

items.title: Gifts with a catch
items.question: A family friend gives you gifts and says you owe them a "special secret" in return. How is this?
items.feedback: Gifts should never come with secrets. This is a warning sign. Tell a trusted adult, even if the person is nice to you.
items.deeper: This is called grooming: someone builds trust with gifts and kindness, then asks for secrets. The gift does not mean you owe them anything.

items.title: Sitting on a lap
items.question: An adult you know asks you to sit on their lap, and you don't want to. How is this?
items.feedback: You can say "No, thank you" and sit somewhere else. Your body belongs to you.
items.deeper: Your body belongs to you, even with adults you know. Saying "no, thank you" politely is not rude.

items.title: Pictures on a phone
items.question: An older cousin shows you pictures on their phone of people without clothes, and says it's a grown-up secret. How is this?
items.feedback: Showing children pictures like this is not okay, even from family. Move away and tell a trusted adult.
items.deeper: Showing private pictures to a child is a kind of abuse, even with no touching. It is never your fault that you saw them.

items.title: A friend's worry
items.question: Your friend tells you an adult has been touching her in a way she doesn't like, and asks you not to tell anyone. How is this?
items.feedback: Your friend is not safe. Tell a trusted adult, even though she asked you not to. That is how a good friend helps.
items.deeper: Some secrets are too big for children to carry. Telling an adult is not betraying your friend; it is getting her help.

items.title: A kiss hello
items.question: Your uncle says you must kiss him hello or you are being rude, and you don't want to. How is this?
items.feedback: You can offer a wave or a handshake instead. Greeting someone kindly doesn't need a kiss.
items.deeper: Respect works both ways. Adults who care about you will accept a different greeting. If someone gets angry, tell a parent.
